title: Dwaraka Welcomes Krishna Home
subtitle: A conch brings the whole city running
story:
Krishna was coming home. He had been away through the great war, and then through the long months among the Pandavas in Hastinapura, and now the city of Dwaraka, his own city by the sea, heard its lord returning before it saw him.

He was still some way out, crossing into his own prosperous land of Anarta, when he lifted his conch and blew. The white-bellied shell, reddened by his lips, sent out a sound that carried ahead of him like light — a sound that, as the verses say, takes the fear out of the world. And Dwaraka, hearing it, rose and ran to meet him.

The citizens poured through the gates, their faces bright with joy, their voices choked with delight. "We bow to your feet, lord," they cried, "feet that Brahma and Shiva and the kings of the gods themselves worship. Be our welfare — for you alone are our mother, our friend, our husband, our father. When you went away to the Kurus, or to the Madhu people, on visits to friends, how could we live? How could we bear it, with your glance far off — the glance that dries up every sorrow?" So the people spoke, and Krishna heard them all, he who is tender to those who love him. And the joy ran through the city like a tide, from the swept avenues to the humblest doorway with its pot of curds.

The city had been made ready for him as for a festival. Arches of welcome stood raised at the gates and along the roads; the great avenues had been swept clean, the lanes and markets and squares freshened; and at every door were set pots of curds and unbroken rice, fruits and sugarcane. Out of the gates came his own people to meet him: his father Vasudeva, great-hearted; Akrura, the wise elder of the clan; Ugrasena, the old king Krishna had restored to his throne; and Balarama, his elder brother — called Rama as well — with his sons Pradyumna and Charudeshna riding behind, and Samba, the son of Queen Jambavati. The foremost elephant led the procession, and the brahmins chanted blessings of good fortune. The women performers of the city rode out by the hundred in their carriages, eager for his sight; actors and dancers, bards and praise-singers filled the road with song.

Krishna moved among them and did not hurry past. He bowed to the elders and to the brahmins with their wives; he took the hands of his relatives, returning embrace for embrace, smile for smile, glance for glance — the whole long welcome answered in kind. The noble women of Dwaraka watched from the terraces along the royal road, saying that fortune itself lived in his chest, and that their eyes could not drink enough of the sight of him. He passed beneath the white umbrella and the waving fans, showered with flowers from the balconies all the way to his father's house.

There his mothers were waiting — the wives of Vasudeva, with Devaki, who had borne him, at their head. He bowed to them, and they lifted him onto their laps and held him like a child again, their eyes wet with the tears of love. For a long moment the courtyard held only the sound of their weeping.

Only then did he enter his own palace, the house that fulfilled every desire. His wives, who had watched the road for his return all the months he was gone, saw their husband come home, and their hearts broke into festival; with their children about them, with their eyes and their very hearts, they embraced their lord. And the verses close the scene with a quiet marvel: even to those who lived beside him, who saw him in the next room and alone, his two feet were always new.

Dwaraka had him back. The sea-girt city, which had been decked and swept and kept awake while he was away, settled into the long happiness of his presence.
reflection: The citizens' words — 'you alone are our mother, our friend, our husband, our father' — are striking because they come from an entire city, not from a single devotee; a whole people measures its safety by one presence. And the closing marvel, that his feet were always new even to those who lived beside him, says something quiet about devotion: nearness does not exhaust wonder.
next_story_tease: But the wheel of time was turning, and the years of peace were numbered.
hero_scene: Krishna sounding his conch at the approach to Dwaraka, the white sea-girt city rising ahead of him, while citizens stream through the decorated gates with garlands, pots of curds and flowers to welcome him home.
